title: Gerson’s proofs: any offense outweighs even annihilation
source_text: XII. Atque hanc suam sententiam in sequentibus multis argumentis confirmat. Nam omnem offensam in Deum de se mortiferam esse probat ex eo quod potest juste a Deo puniri poena mortis, tam temporalis quam aeternae; imo annihilationis poena. Et hoc quia nulla poena talis ita mala est, quantum mala est quaevis offensa Dei. Mortem autem & annihilationem non esse tam malam, quam ipsam Dei offensam, inde deducit, quod potius toleranda esset omnis mors poenalis & annihilatio, quam committenda quantumlibet parva offensa in Deum, quoniam opposito dato, dari posset casus in quo offensa Dei licite fieri posset. Nempe, si aliter vitari non posset mors & annihilatio.
pass_a_gloss: And he confirms this his opinion in what follows by many arguments. For he proves that every offense against God is of itself deadly from this, that it can justly be punished by God with the penalty of death, both temporal and eternal—nay, with the penalty of annihilation. And this because no such penalty is so evil as any offense of God is evil. But that death and annihilation are not so evil as the offense of God itself, he deduces from this, that every penal death and annihilation ought rather to be endured than even the least offense against God committed, because if the opposite were granted, a case could be given in which an offense of God could lawfully be done—namely, if death and annihilation could not otherwise be avoided.
pass_b_english: Gerson argues any offense against God can justly draw death—even annihilation—because no penalty matches that evil.
Better suffer any punishment than commit the slightest offense against God; else offense could become licit to avoid death.

choices.why: Extreme penal foil in Gerson’s a fortiori.
